author: g. f. rosas
title: Bryan Rust reflects on Evgeni Malkin's career and legacy with Penguins
text:
Evgeni Malkin’s future was a major topic of discussion in the Pittsburgh Penguins locker room during cleanout day, according to Bryan Rust on May 27. When asked about Malkin, Rust said, “All I’m going to say about that is, I love Geno. I love Geno as a friend and as a teammate. I don’t know life in the NHL without him.”
With Malkin now officially signed for another year, Rust shared his perspective while preparing for a summer skate in Cranberry. “I mean, from my point of view, I don’t think there was ever a doubt. But obviously, I don’t sit at the table upstairs, I don’t make those decisions, I’m not in on those conversations,” Rust said. “Obviously, Geno was incredible this past year, and you can see he just loves being in this room, he loves playing the game, he loves this city, he loves the fans.”
Rust described witnessing Malkin’s impact both as an opponent and later as a teammate. As a teenager growing up near Detroit and supporting the Red Wings during their Stanley Cup Finals matchups against Pittsburgh in 2008 and 2009, Rust admitted: “So, I was not a fan of Geno.” He recalled watching from home as Detroit won one year before seeing Pittsburgh claim victory the next season—led by Malkin’s performance that earned him Playoff MVP honors at age 22.
After being drafted by Pittsburgh in 2010 and spending time developing his game through college hockey and minor leagues before joining the Penguins roster full-time in the 2014-15 season, Rust said any negative feelings toward Malkin changed: “It was just excitement of obviously a team that had won and had world-class players like Geno… It’s a locker room that you step into, and you almost just want to get autographs because those guys are so awesome.”
Rust reflected on memorable moments alongside Malkin since becoming teammates: “I think there were so many instances where he would take over games… it was always so much fun to just watch him completely take over a game… That’s a rare breed.” On maintaining elite play with one franchise for more than two decades—a rarity among professional athletes—Rust added: “Sometimes guys wear out their welcome… But obviously Geno… that wouldn’t happen to them here because of the way that this organization and the city has treated them… This place is home for G.” The Pittsburgh Penguins have achieved numerous playoff appearances with contributions from Hall of Fame players such as Malkin; they form an important part of local sports culture with strong community ties; they host games at PPG Paints Arena under ownership by Fenway Sports Group—all according to, the official website .
